title: OVERDRIVE: overcoming cancer cell resistance to drugs by supplementary nontoxic molecule predicted by a machine learning tool
projectDescription: Here we aim to test the notion that overcoming cancer cells’ acquired resistance to chemotherapy drugs may be achieved by administrating together with the main drug a molecule that is not toxic by itself but enhances the drug efficacy in killing the resistant cells. Finding such a supplementary molecule is a nontrivial task. Our algorithmic approach, named OVERcoming Drug Resistance by In Vitro cell Exposure (OVERDRIVE), involves exposing drug-sensitive cancer cells to increasing drug concentrations for several weeks followed by a comprehensive proteomic analysis of both the exposed and sensitive cells. Applying a machine learning tool Genome Enhancer to the proteomic data reveals the protein network accounting for the differences between the exposed and naïve cells and predicts molecules that may shift the exposed cell phenotypes to the sensitive one. Experimental validation of the top predicted nontoxic molecules confirmed that the combined treatment of the experimental drug LTCA2940 that targets redox pathways with identified supplementary molecule restored the sensitivity of LTCA2940-resistant cells. The OVERDRIVE approach may pave a way for a strategy to overcoming anticancer resistance to chemotherapy in clinic.
sampleProcessingProtocol: Cancer cells line were treated with gradually increasing concentrations of cancer drugs to develop resistance. Proteomics assays were employed to acquire differences between sensitive and resistant cells on the protein level.
dataProcessingProtocol: Raw data files with LC-MS/MS results were submitted to Proteome Discoverer 3.1 for processing. The peak integration m/z tolerance was 20 ppm and the target false discovery rate (FDR) was set at 0.05. Mascot (Matrix Science, UK) search engine was used with oxidation (M), deamidation (NQ), acetyl (N-terminal), carbamidomethyl (C) and N-ethylmaleimide (C) being dynamic modifications. Protein abundances were used for the determination of the expression differences. Only proteins identified with high or medium confidence by two or more peptides were accepted, with contaminant proteins being filtered out. The relative abundances determined via TMT reporter ions were normalized by the sum for all abundances in the TMT channel. Fold changes were calculated as the resistant/sensitive ratios of the normalized abundances. Changes in the redox state of a peptide with cysteine were determined by dividing the peptide fold change by the expression fold change of the protein to which it belongs. The two-sided, unpaired student’s t-test was used to calculate p-values for the differences between the sensitive and resistant cells. The final results were presented as Excel tables containing protein fold changes for PISA and Express analyses and peptide fold changes for redox analysis, together with the corresponding p-values for all analysis types. The proteomic datasets were processed through Genome Enhancer (https://genexplain.com/genome-enhancer) that yielded shortlists of candidate supp-molecules for the tested drugs.
